title.en: The Brahmajala Sutta: Buddha and the Sixty-Two Views

region.en: Ambalatthika royal rest-house between Rajagaha and Nalanda (symbolic pin at Rajagaha)
region.zh: 王舍城與那爛陀之間的芒果苗驛館（以王舍城為象徵定位）

texts.period: Composed c. 4th-3rd c. BCE, Pali canon written 1st c. BCE; Rhys Davids translation 1899

source.work: Dialogues of the Buddha, trans. T. W. & C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1899-1921), Sutta 1 (Brahmajala Sutta, Dialogues vol. I)

summary.en: Criticized by a hostile teacher and praised by that teacher's own pupil, the Buddha tells the monks not to be moved by either. He then surveys the whole cosmos of sects, classifying sixty-two theories about soul and world, and shows how the 'I am the creator' delusion of Great Brahma arises whenever a world-system re-evolves.
summary.zh: 有師徒二人一路隨行，師毀佛而弟子讚佛，佛陀囑咐僧眾毀譽皆不可動心。經中歷數外道關於我與世的六十二種見解，並講述世界成壞之際梵天自認造物主的妄見緣起，以「真理之網」總攝一切戲論。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); canonical prose is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Traveling with five hundred monks between Rajagaha and Nalanda, the Buddha lodged for the night in the royal rest-house of the Ambalatthika garden. A wandering teacher named Suppiya and his pupil Brahmadatta had followed the company all day, the master deriding the Buddha, his doctrine and his Order, while the disciple praised them in the same measure. At dawn the monks discussed the spectacle, and the Buddha, overhearing, told them neither to burn with anger at criticism nor to swell with pride at praise. Praise built only on outward conduct was shallow; the true praise of a Buddha concerns deeper things, knowledge that a Tathagata alone can reach by realizing them for himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta (Rhys Davids 1899); not verbatim.

passages.text: He explained how some cosmological doctrines arise. Sooner or later a world-system passes away, and beings are reborn mostly in the World of Radiance, mind-made, feeding on joy, shining from themselves. When the system re-evolves, the empty Brahma palace appears; a being whose merit is exhausted falls from Radiance into it and, dwelling alone so long, begins to long for company. Other beings then fall into the palace as his companions. The first-born concludes: 'I am Brahma, the Great Brahma, the Supreme, the Maker, the Creator, the Father of all that are and are to be; these others are of my creation.' The newcomers agree that he made them, and a later such being reborn among men recalls only that birth and teaches that Brahma is eternal while his creatures are not.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta (Rhys Davids 1899); not verbatim.

passages.text: Around this core the sutta lays out the sixty-two views: eternalists who claim soul and world are everlasting; semi-eternalists of four kinds; extensionists who declare the world finite, infinite or neither; eel-wrigglers who equivocate for fear of being caught in error; fortuitous-originationists who say everything arises by chance; sixteen kinds of conscious-survivalists, eight who say the soul after death is unconscious, eight who say it is neither, seven annihilationists, and five prophets of bliss in this very life. Every one of them, the Buddha says, is manufactured out of what is felt through sense-contact: from contact comes feeling, from feeling craving, and from craving the renewed becoming that keeps the wheels of rebirth turning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta (Rhys Davids 1899); not verbatim.

passages.text: All who speculate about past and future, however they flounder this way and that, are caught in this one net, just as a fine-meshed net swept over a little pool catches every fish in it. Only the Tathagata stands outside it: his outward form remains visible so long as he lives, but the tie that binds it to rebirth is cut, as when the stalk of a bunch of mangoes is severed and the fruit goes with it. When Ananda asked what the discourse should be called, the Buddha named it the Net of Theories, the Supreme Net, the Glorious Victory in the day of battle; and when it ended, the thousandfold world-system shook.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta (Rhys Davids 1899); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mahasamaya Sutta: The Great Gathering of the Gods

region.en: The Great Wood, Kapilavatthu, home city of the Sakyans (symbolic pin at Lumbini)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛釋迦族故里大林（以藍毘尼為象徵定位）

texts.period: Composed c. 4th-3rd c. BCE, Pali canon written 1st c. BCE; Rhys Davids translation 1910

source.work: Dialogues of the Buddha, trans. T. W. & C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1899-1921), Sutta 20 (Mahasamaya Suttanta, Dialogues vol. II)

summary.en: Dwelling at Kapilavatthu with five hundred arahants, the Buddha is visited by gods of the ten thousand world-systems and recites a grand catalog naming the hosts of deities, from local yakkhas and the Four Great Kings to nagas, asuras and Great Brahma himself. Mara rises with his army to seize the assembly by lust, but finds nothing to grasp and recoils.
summary.zh: 佛陀在迦毘羅衛大林與五百阿羅漢同住，萬界諸天咸來集會。佛陀唱名誦出夜叉、四天王、乾闥婆、龍、阿修羅、諸天乃至大梵天等神眾名號，最後魔軍欲以貪慾縛眾僧，卻無隙可乘，敗退而去。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); canonical prose is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Dwelling at Kapilavatthu in the Great Wood with five hundred arahants, the Buddha was visited by gods of the ten thousand world-systems. Four gods of the Pure Abodes came down 'as easily as a strong man might stretch out his arm' and recited verses before him: 'Great is the gathering in the glade! The hosts of heaven together met! We too are come unto this congress blest, and fain would see the Company Invincible.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 20, Mahasamaya Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Buddha then announced that he would recite the names of the celestial hosts. Seven thousand yakkhas of the country, six thousand from Himalaya and three thousand from Sata's Hill arrived, sixteen thousand in all, and Kumbhira of Rajagaha came with a hundred thousand in his train. The Four Great Kings arrived from the four quarters: Dhatarattha of the East, lord of the gandhabbas; Virulhaka of the South, lord of the kumbhandas; Virupakkha of the West, lord of the nagas; and Kuvera of the North, lord of the yakkhas, each with sons all named after Indra, standing in the wood shedding effulgence in every direction.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 20, Mahasamaya Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: After them came the gandhabba chiefs; the nagas and the harpies who prey on them, yet had been tamed by the Buddha's protection; the asura host with Rahu, Vepacitti and the spirit of Evil, Namuci; the gods of Fire, Water, Earth and Air, Varuna and Soma, the Yama twins, the fairies of Moon and Sun, and Sakka the Generous, Lord of the Vasus. Sixty spirit hosts of diverse hue were counted, and beyond them gods past reckoning, all come rejoicing to the forest glade to see the brethren met together there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 20, Mahasamaya Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Great Brahma, suzerain of a thousand worlds, arrived with ten Brahma-lords and his retinue. Then Mara rose with his swarthy army: 'Come on and seize and bind these; let all be bound by lust! Surround them on every side and let not one escape!' He smote the ground with his palm with a din like a thundercloud big with rain, then recoiled, still raging, powerless to effect anything. The Master warned his monks, and they stood alert; where no lust was found, nor a hair of whose body stirred, the foe departed empty. All creation rejoiced with the victors.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 20, Mahasamaya Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Agganna Sutta: How the World Cycles and Kings Are Elected
title.zh: 太初經：世界成壞與民選初王

region.en: Savatthi, East Park, the mansion of Migara's mother

texts.period: Composed c. 4th-3rd c. BCE, Pali canon written 1st c. BCE; C. A. F. Rhys Davids translation 1921

source.work: Dialogues of the Buddha, trans. T. W. & C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1899-1921), Sutta 27 (Agganna Suttanta, Dialogues vol. III)

summary.en: Called shavelings by the brahmins they left, two novices are answered with the Buddhist cosmogony: luminous beings from the Radiant heaven descend when the world re-forms, taste the savoury earth, grow greedy, and through greed and pride the sun, moon, rice, sexes, houses, property, theft and law arise. The people then elect the first king, Mahasammata the Great Elect, and every caste is traced to human function, not divine birth.
summary.zh: 兩位出身婆羅門的沙彌被本族人咒罵，佛陀以佛教自身的創世敘事作答：世界成壞之際，光音天眾生下生人間，先食地味，因貪而日月星辰顯現，繼而穀物、兩性、屋舍、田界、盜與刑相繼出現；人民公選摩訶三末多為最初之王，四姓皆出於職分而非梵天所生，法為最勝。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); canonical prose is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: At Savatthi, in the East Park mansion built by Migara's mother, two brahmin novices, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, complained that the brahmins reviled them for deserting 'the best class' for shaveling friars. The Buddha answered that brahmin women plainly conceive, bear and nurse children, so the boast of being born from Brahma's mouth is a travesty of the god; the four classes alike contain both scoundrels and saints, and whoever becomes an arahant is chief, for a norm (dhamma), not birth, is the standard: 'The Dhamma is the best among this folk, both in this life and in the next.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 27, Agganna Suttanta (C. A. F. Rhys Davids 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he told how a world-system, sooner or later, passes away, when beings are mostly reborn in the World of Radiance, mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, traversing the air, abiding long in glory. Sooner or later the world begins to re-evolve, and those beings come to life here as humans, still made of mind. At that time all is one world of water, dark and blinding; no moon nor sun, no stars or constellations, no night or day, months or years appear, and beings are reckoned simply as beings. Presently earth with its savour spreads over the waters like the scum on cooling boiled rice-gruel, coloured like fine ghee, sweet as unblended honey.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 27, Agganna Suttanta (C. A. F. Rhys Davids 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: A being of greedy disposition touched the savoury earth with a finger, tasted it, and craving entered him; the others followed, and as they ate lumps of the earth their self-luminance faded, whereupon moon and sun, constellations, night and day, months and years became manifest. Their bodies grew solid; the comely despised the ill-favoured, and through their vanity the food vanished. Mushroom-like outgrowths arose and disappeared, then sweet creepers, then rice ripening wild and self-renewing in open ground. When female and male features appeared, passion arose between beings, and the shamed pair were pelted with sand, ashes and cowdung; huts were built to conceal what had become immoral.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 27, Agganna Suttanta (C. A. F. Rhys Davids 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: A lazy being then gathered rice for two meals at once, then for many days, and hoarded rice grew husk and stopped regrowing. The rice fields were divided and bounded; a greedy being stole another's plot, and stealing, censure, lying and punishment came into the world. The beings then chose the handsomest, most capable one as Great Elect, Mahasammata, paying him a share of rice, 'chosen by the people' being the meaning of his name. Nobles, brahmins, tradesfolk and hunters alike trace back to those same primordial beings, by function and not by blood; whoever does evil falls to woe whoever he be, and the arahant is chief, and the Buddha declared that he himself was that first Great Elect.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 27, Agganna Suttanta (C. A. F. Rhys Davids 1921); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. A. F. Rhys Davids, 'Agganna Suttanta: A Book of Genesis', Dialogues of the Buddha III, PTS 1921

narrative.en: The Agganna Sutta begins as a debate about caste and ends as the fullest cosmogony in the Pali canon. Two young brahmins, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, have gone forth from their families to become monks under the Buddha, and their kinsmen abuse them for it: only brahmins, they say, are of the best class, of pure complexion, true children of Brahma, born from his mouth, his offspring and his heirs. The Buddha's retort is practical and satirical at once: brahmin women are known to be fertile, seen to be with child, bringing forth and nursing babies. Whoever claims a mouth-birth from the god 'makes a travesty of the nature of Brahma.' Looking at the four classes, nobles, brahmins, tradesfolk and workpeople, one finds thieves, liars and libertines in each, and also the virtuous in each. Since good and evil are distributed without regard to lineage, the wise do not admit the brahmins' claim. Whoever of any class becomes an arahant, free of the intoxicants, is chief; and a norm, the Dhamma, is 'the best among this folk, both in this life and in the next.' As proof he cites King Pasenadi of Kosala, who bows to the Buddha not from weakness but because he honours the Dhamma. Having established Dhamma rather than descent as the standard, the Buddha then does what no other early text does so completely: he tells how the world itself comes to be. There comes a time when the world-system passes away, and beings are mostly reborn in the World of Radiance (Abhassara), where they dwell made of mind, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, traversing the air, remaining long in glory. Sooner or later the world begins to re-evolve, and beings who had deceased from the World of Radiance come to life again, still mind-made, luminous and aerial. At that time all is one world of water, dark and of darkness that makes blind: no moon or sun, no stars or constellations, no night or day, no months, half-months, years or seasons, and neither female nor male; beings are reckoned simply as beings. Then, after a long time, earth with its savour spreads out in the waters, exactly as a scum forms on the surface of boiled milky rice that is cooling. It has colour like well-made ghee, odour, and sweetness like flawless honeycomb. A being of greedy disposition, curious, tastes the savoury earth with a finger. Craving enters him, and others follow his example, breaking off lumps with their hands. From that eating the self-luminance of those beings fades away, and as it fades the moon and sun become manifest, then the star-shapes and constellations, then night and day, months and half-months, seasons and years. Feeding on the earth, their bodies grow solid and their complexions diverge; the better-favoured despise the worse, and in their vanity the savoury earth itself disappears. They weep for it, and their cry survives as a primordial saying. Mushroom-like outgrowths arise next, sweet as honey, and vanish the same way when pride in beauty spreads; then sweet creepers; then rice ripening in open spaces without powder or husk, fragrant and clean-grained, standing ripe again each morning where it was plucked the evening before. With rice, the sexes differentiate, passion arises, and the onlookers pelt the offending pair with sand, ashes and cowdung, crying 'Perish, foul one!' The text notes that bridal showers of sand and dust in his own day repeat this primordial gesture unknowingly. Shamed, the immoral build huts to conceal what they do, and houses, in effect, are born. Then laziness changes everything: one being, unwilling to make two trips, gathers rice for two meals at once, then for more and more days. Hoarded rice acquires husk and powder, the cut stems stand in stubble and grow no more. The beings bewail their evil customs and divide off the rice fields, setting boundaries. A greedy being watches his own plot and steals another's; caught and warned, he repeats the theft, and men smite him with hands, clods and sticks. With that beginning, stealing, censure, lying and punishment all become known. The crisis produces government. The beings gather and resolve to select one being who should be wrathful when indignation is right, censure what should rightly be censured and banish who deserves banishment, and they will pay him a proportion of the rice. They choose the handsomest, best-favoured, most attractive and most capable among them. 'Chosen by the whole people' (maha-janasammuti) is the meaning of Mahasammata, the Great Elect, the first standing phrase for a king; Khattiya (noble) means 'lord of the fields'; and Raja means 'he who charms the others by the Norm.' Kingship here is neither divine right nor conquest: it is a compact of consent, paid for in rice. The other estates are etymologized in the same spirit: Brahmins are those who 'put away' evil and immoral customs (bholetti), dwelling in leaf huts in the woods, meditating (jhayaka), while those who could not endure meditation settled at the village edges, making books, the Veda-repeating ajjhayaka, 'looked upon as the lowest then, thought the best now.' The Vessas adopt the married state and set on foot various trades; the Suddas take to hunting. The sutta closes the circle back to its opening argument. From all four classes, whoever misprizes his own estate may go forth into the homeless life, so the company of recluses too is of human, not divine origin. And karma respects no birth: a khattiya, brahmin, vessa or sudda who lives ill is reborn in the Waste, the Woeful Way, the Downfall, Purgatory; who lives well is reborn in a happy, bright world; the arahant of any of the four classes is chief, in virtue of a norm. The Buddha quotes and endorses Brahma the Eternal Youth's stanza: the khattiya is best among those who trust in lineage, but one clothed in wisdom and virtue is best of all among spirits and men. Then comes the quiet thunderclap of the whole discourse: the Great Elect of that first age, the Buddha says, was not another person. 'I at that time was Mahasammata.' The first king of the world, ancestor of the Sakyan line, is the Buddha himself in a former life, and the descendants of Vasettha and Bharadvaja who insult them are, on the Buddha's own showing, his own heirs. The story functions on three levels at once. As polemic, it dissolves the brahmins' creation-claim by out-creating them: if there must be a genesis, it is a genesis of greed, not of ritual purity. As social theory, it is one of the earliest contract accounts of sovereignty on record: law, punishment and monarchy all arise from property disputes, and the king is an employee of the people. As cosmology, it naturalizes the cosmos: sun, moon and stars are not makers but by-products, manifest only when the beings' own light fails through craving. Rhys Davids saw in it 'a book of genesis' worthy of comparison with any in world literature; modern scholarship (Gethin, Collins) reads it as the canonical charter for Buddhism's characteristic amalgam of cyclical time, karma and an ethic that measures people by deeds rather than birth.
narrative.zh: 太初經（阿攝毱義）始於種姓之辯，終於巴利聖典中最完整的創世論。婆羅門自稱梵天之口所生、種姓最貴，佛答以婆羅門婦人明明懷胎生子，此說實為誣梵；四姓皆有善惡，證阿羅漢者最尊，法為準繩。隨後佛說世界成壞：劫壞時眾生生光音天，以心為體、自放光明、飛行空中；劫復成時，下生為人。其時惟一水世界，冥暗無日月星辰，無晝夜歲時，亦無男女。久之，地味遍於水上，如熟乳糜之凝皮，色如酥，味如蜜。有貪者以指嘗之，貪愛遂生，眾競食之，自光漸隱，日月星辰、晝夜歲月乃現。身漸粗澀，美者鄙陋者，地味以驕而滅；繼生蕈、蔓，皆驕而滅；復生自熟之米。男女形現，欲念熾然，眾擲沙土牛糞於淫者，為蔽其醜乃造屋。懶者併取兩餐，積糧愈多，米遂生糠穀不復更生；眾乃分田立界，有竊他田者，於是盜、訶、妄語、刑罰並出。眾遂公選最俊慧者為王，授以稻分，是名摩訶三末多（大眾所選）；剎帝利者田主，剎利者以法化他。婆羅門者言除惡不善法，林中結菴而禪者曰禪人，不能禪者居村造書、諷誦吠陀。商賈興貿易，首陀羅事漁獵。凡四姓行惡者墮惡趣，行善者生善處，證阿羅漢者最尊。佛引梵童子偈而自承：彼時之大眾選王，即我前身。世間初王非神授，乃民約；日月非造物，乃貪食之餘燼；種姓非天生，乃職分之名。

functions: Anti-caste charter: rebirth to hell or heaven follows deeds, not lineage; the arahant of any class is chief
Cosmogony of the Pali canon: cyclical world-evolution, mind-made luminous beings, and food (greed) as the engine of differentiation
Contract theory of kingship: Mahasammata elected by the people and paid in rice; law and punishment arising from property disputes
Etiological folk etymologies: explains primordial sayings, bridal dust-throwing, the lament 'alas, the savour', and the names of the four varnas

variants.name: Brahmajala world-evolution passage (DN 1)
variants.text_tradition: Theravada, Digha Nikaya 1, a verbatim parallel passage on the dissolution and re-evolution of world-systems and the Radiant Abode
variants.summary: The same stock cosmology (world dissolves, beings in the World of Radiance, world re-evolves) appears in the Brahmajala Sutta to explain how the Great Brahma delusion arises; the Agganna version adds the earth, food and society sequence.

variants.name: Chinese Dirghagama parallel (Sutra of Origins, 'Fo kaai jieh fan chi a bahn ching')
variants.text_tradition: Dharmaguptaka/Chinese canon, Chang A-han (Taisho no. 1), a parallel to DN 27 transmitted in Chinese translation
variants.summary: A parallel telling of the Radiant beings descending, the savoury earth, the arising of sexes, houses, property and the election of the first king, confirming that the myth circulated across early schools.

variants.name: Samyutta-Nikaya echoes on the world-cycle
variants.text_tradition: Theravada, Samyutta Nikaya (e.g. S. III on the mind-made luminous beings) and Itivuttaka parallels on giving and rebirth
variants.summary: Shorter canonical echoes of the same cosmology and of karma-over-caste ethics; none carries the full descent-and-election story.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: Canonical scripture of a living Theravada tradition, still chanted and taught in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand and the diaspora. The caste-refutation is quoted in modern equality debates, including Ambedkarite Buddhism; cite by sutta number and PTS reference, and avoid retelling the election of Mahasammata as a slur on either brahmins or monarchy — the text itself ends with praise for lineage and virtue together.

title.en: The Cakkavatti-Sihanada Sutta: The Wheel-King, the Sword-Age and Maitreya
title.zh: 轉輪聖王師子吼經：衰減之世與彌勒

region.en: Matula village, land of the Magadhese (symbolic pin at Rajagaha)
region.zh: 摩竭陀國摩突羅村（以王舍城為象徵定位）

texts.period: Composed c. 4th-3rd c. BCE, Pali canon written 1st c. BCE; C. A. F. Rhys Davids translation 1921

source.work: Dialogues of the Buddha, trans. T. W. & C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1899-1921), Sutta 26 (Cakkavatti-Sihanada Suttanta, Dialogues vol. III)

summary.en: The Buddha tells how the wheel-turning king's celestial Wheel is not inherited but won by the Ariyan duty of giving wealth to the destitute; when a later king hoards, poverty, theft, execution and violence cascade until lifespans halve from eighty thousand years to ten. After a seven-day sword-period in which kin kill kin, survivors resolve on goodness, lifespans climb again, and in the renewed world the future Buddha Metteyya (Maitreya) will arise under the wheel-king Sankha.
summary.zh: 佛說轉輪聖王之天輪非世襲而有，乃由施貧困者之正法王道感得；後王不行其道，貧窮、偷盜、刑戮相尋，人壽自八萬歲遞減至十歲，刀兵劫起，親屬相殘。七日之後，倖存者誓不再殺，人壽倍增，閻浮提城郭相接，未來彌勒佛將於螺王治世之時出世。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the sword-period passage parallels apocalyptic flood-and-renewal myths across traditions and is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: In the Magadhan village of Matula the Buddha bade the monks live as islands and refuges unto themselves, with the Norm as their refuge, and to keep to their own pastures where their fathers roamed. Then he told of King Strongtyre (Dalhanemi), a righteous wheel-turning monarch who ruled the four quarters by righteousness, possessed of the seven treasures and more than a thousand hero sons. After ages the celestial Wheel slipped down from its place; the king, knowing the Wheel was no paternal heritage, handed the earth to his son, shaved hair and beard, donned yellow robes and went forth, and on the seventh day the Wheel vanished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 26, Cakkavatti-Sihanada Suttanta (C. A. F. Rhys Davids 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The grieving heir was told by the royal hermit that the Wheel is won, not inherited: the Ariyan duty of a wheel-turner is to lean on the Norm, honouring it as banner and master, to provide watch and ward for one's own folk, army, court, brahmins and householders, town and country, the religious world, even beasts and birds; to let no wrongdoing prevail in the kingdom, and to give wealth to whosoever in the kingdom is poor. Performed on the full-moon feast, the duty brought the thousand-spoked Wheel back, and the king followed it east, south, west and north; at every halt the rival kings welcomed him crying 'All is thine, O mighty king! Teach us!' and he answered only: slay no living thing, take nothing not given, no wrong touching bodily desires, speak no lie, drink no maddening drink.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 26, Cakkavatti-Sihanada Suttanta (C. A. F. Rhys Davids 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seven such kings reigned; then came one who, though he asked the keepers of the Ariyan duty for its content, bestowed no wealth on the destitute. Poverty grew rife; a starving man stole, and the king, having first paid each thief, at last began executing them. Hearing of the sword, folk armed themselves to rob and murder. Thus from goods not bestowed came poverty, from poverty stealing, from stealing violence, murder, lying, slander, adultery, covetousness, wrong views and broken piety, each stage halving the span of life from eighty thousand years, through twenty thousand, five hundred and two and a half centuries, to a mere ten years, when maidens of five are marriageable, the word for 'moral' is unknown, and kudrusa grain is the noblest food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 26, Cakkavatti-Sihanada Suttanta (C. A. F. Rhys Davids 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Among such humans a sword-period of seven days arises: mothers toward children, children toward mothers, brother toward brother see each other as the sportsman sees his game, and sharp swords appear ready to their hands. Some flee to dens of grass, tree holes, river fastnesses and mountain clefts, living on jungle roots and fruit; emerging at the week's end they embrace, crying 'Hail, O mortal, that thou livest still!' and resolve to abstain from taking life. Lifespans then double generation by generation back up to eighty thousand years. Then Jambudipa is thick with towns a cock could fly between, Benares becomes royal Ketumati, Sankha arises as righteous wheel-king, and the Exalted One Metteyya, a Buddha even as the speaker is now, proclaims the truth; Sankha, rearing the old fairy palace, gives it away and, going forth under Metteyya, wins the supreme goal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 26, Cakkavatti-Sihanada Suttanta (C. A. F. Rhys Davids 1921); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. A. F. Rhys Davids, 'Cakkavatti-Sihanada Suttanta: War, Wickedness, and Wealth', Dialogues of the Buddha III, PTS 1921

narrative.en: The Cakkavatti-Sihanada Sutta, the Lion-roar on the Turning of the Wheel, opens with one of the most quoted lines in the canon: live as islands unto yourselves, as refuges unto yourselves, taking no other refuge, with the Dhamma as your island; and keep to your own pastures, the haunts where your fathers roamed, so that Mara finds no landing-place. From this pastoral preamble the Buddha launches into a cosmological history of kingship that is also an eschatology of the human race. Long ago there reigned a sovereign overlord named Dalhanemi, whom the translator renders Strongtyre: a righteous king ruling in righteousness, lord of the four quarters, possessor of the seven treasures, the Wheel, the Elephant, the Horse, the Gem, the Woman, the House-father and the Counsellor, with more than a thousand hero sons, ruling not by scourge or sword but by righteousness. After many thousand years the Celestial Wheel, the mark of his office, sank down and slipped from its place. Knowing that this signalled not defeat but the end of his tenure, the king installed his eldest son and went forth into the homeless life; and on the seventh day the Wheel vanished like an extinguished lamp. The heir was grieved, but the royal hermit explained the sutta's central doctrine: the Wheel is no paternal heritage. It is won by performing the Ariyan duty of a wheel-turning monarch, and the Buddha spells that duty out with a precision that later Theravada political thought took as constitutional law: lean on the Norm, honour and revere it, be a Norm-banner and Norm-signal, with the Norm as master; provide watch, ward and protection for your own folk, army, nobles, vassals, brahmins and householders, town and country dwellers, the religious world, and beasts and birds; let no wrongdoing prevail anywhere in your kingdom; and whosoever in the kingdom is poor, to him let wealth be given. The performed duty summons the thousand-spoked Wheel back on the full-moon feast, and the king, sprinkling water over it with a ceremonial pitcher, cries: Roll onward, O lord Wheel! The Wheel rolls east, south, west and north, plunging into and rising from the oceans, and wherever it stops the rival kings come with joy and trust, asking only for instruction, which the king gives in five clauses: kill no living thing, take nothing not given, no wrong touching bodily desires, no lie, no maddening drink. Conquest here is a parody, as the translator notes, of the Assyrian or Hun model of empire: the conquered ask to be taught, not merely spared. Seven such monarchs reign. The eighth, though he asks his ministers for the Ariyan duty, does the one thing the formula forbids: he protects, but he bestows no wealth on the destitute. The consequences unfold with the fatality of physics, as the commentator's simile of the lightning-struck tree suggests: a man doing his best shelters under a tree and is killed by the lightning it attracts. Poverty grows rife. A starving man steals; the king, told he steals from hunger, pays him. Hearing that theft pays, others steal; the king, alarmed, reverses himself and has a thief beheaded with drum and rope through the crossroads. Hearing of the sword, men arm themselves and turn to highway robbery and murder. From then on the sermon descends in a litany of cause and effect that the text repeats like an incantation: from goods not bestowed, poverty; from poverty, stealing; from stealing, violence; from violence, murder; then lying, evil speech, adultery, abusive and idle talk, covetousness and ill-will, false opinions, incest, wanton greed, and the collapse of filial piety. With each stage the human span of life and the comeliness of bodies halve: eighty thousand years becomes forty, twenty, ten, five, two and a half thousand, a thousand, five hundred, two and a half centuries, a single century, and finally ten years, when girls of five are marriageable, ghee, butter, oil, sugar and salt have vanished from the earth, kudrusa grain is the highest food, and there is no word for moral among men, far less any moral agent. Homage flows to the unfilial; the world falls into promiscuity like goats and swine and jackals. Then comes the catastrophe the sutta is remembered for, the sword-period (satthantara-kappa) of seven days. Keen mutual enmity becomes the rule, passionate thoughts of killing between mother and child, father and child, brother and sister, each regarding the other as a sportsman regards his game; sharp swords appear ready to their hands and each thinks 'this is a wild beast' and strikes. Some beings, seeing the abyss, hide for those seven days in dens of grass, jungle thickets, tree holes, river fastnesses and mountain clefts, subsisting on roots and fruit. Emerging, they embrace one another, comfort one another and cry: Hail, O mortal, that thou livest still! O happy sight, to find thee still alive! The survivors reason that the heavy loss of kith and kin came from evil ways, and resolve, step by step, to abstain from taking life, then from taking what is not given, adultery, lying, evil speech, abuse, covetousness, ill-will and false opinion, and to restore filial and religious piety. The moral ledger then runs in reverse: lifespan and comeliness double generation by generation, ten years to twenty, forty, eighty, down the same column it fell, until humans live eighty thousand years again, marriageable at five hundred, troubled only by appetite, non-assimilation and old age. The renewed world is described with an almost comic concreteness: Jambudipa (India) becomes mighty and prosperous, villages, towns and royal cities so close that a cock could fly from each one to the next, mankind pervading it as a jungle is pervaded by reeds; eighty-four thousand towns with Ketumati, Benares under a new name, as royal city. There a wheel-turning king named Sankha arises, righteous, lord of the four quarters, possessor of the seven treasures. At that period, the sutta predicts, an Exalted One named Metteyya, Arahant, Fully Awakened, abounding in wisdom and goodness, will arise in the world, a teacher of gods and men even as the speaker is now, attended by thousands of monks rather than hundreds. King Sankha will raise up again the fairy palace which King Great Panada had built and which had sunk in the Ganges; he will dwell in it, then give it away to recluses, brahmins, the destitute, wayfarers and beggars; and he himself, cutting off hair and beard, will go forth under Metteyya and, alone and zealous, attain that supreme goal while yet in this visible world. The sutta then loops back to its opening exhortation, giving the monk's own version of the wheel-turner's fourfold growth: length of years through the Roads to Power, comeliness through discipline, happiness through the jhanas, and wealth, paradoxically, through pervading the four quarters with a mind charged with love, pity, sympathy and equanimity. As myth, the sutta stands with the great decline-and-renewal narratives of world literature: a civilizational collapse driven neither by gods nor monsters but by an unsorted moral economy, a survival through hiding (as flood-heroes survive in a box or a cave), a covenant of the survivors, and a paradise whose price is the very virtue the catastrophe taught. Its political afterlife is immense: Buddhist kings in Sri Lanka, Burma and Thailand ruled in the wheel-king's shadow, and the Metteyya prophecy remains the living eschatology of Theravada villages. The world-renewal motif here is not a flood of water but a flood of blades, and the renewal is not divine rescue but a change of heart.
narrative.zh: 轉輪聖王師子吼經以「自作洲渚、自作歸依」始，以人類的衰減與更新終。往昔有轉輪王強硬螺（質呾羅末尼? 譯名從強硬螺），七寶具足，以法而治；歲久天輪下沉，王知此非失位之凶，乃傳位太子，剃髮染衣出家，七日而輪隱沒。太子悲泣，隱者告之：天輪非父業可承，當行轉輪王之正法王道，依於法、敬重法、以法為幢，護念自己之民、軍旅、宮廷、婆羅門居士、城邑村野、沙門乃至禽獸，國中不使有一非法，貧者與財。王如是行，望月齋戒之宵天輪復現，千輻具足；王以瓶水灑輪曰「轉進，天輪！」輪游四洲，敵王皆願受教，王唯授五戒。如是七王相繼；第八王雖問正法，而不施貧者，於是貧窮滋盛，貧則盜，王初酬盜，後乃誅之，眾聞而帶刀行劫，由是殺、妄語、兩舌、邪淫、貪瞋邪見遞增，人壽自八萬歲每況減半，至十歲，五歲女可行嫁，酥油糖鹽不存，人間無善名。其時刀兵劫起，七日之中母子兄弟相視如鹿，鋒刃在手，相殺無赦；有避入草莽、樹孔、河洲、山窟，食草根果實，七日出而相抱相慰曰「賀汝得全！」遂誓不殺生，善法漸增，壽命倍增至八萬歲。爾時閻浮提城邑相望，雞飛得度，波羅奈改名迦提沫底，八萬四千城，螺王以法治世；彌勒如來應供等正覺出世，千數比丘圍繞；螺王重興大波那陀天王之天宮，布施已，從彌勒出家，即生證阿羅漢果。經末還原僧事：四神變、四梵住即比丘之壽、色、樂、力。

functions: Theory of legitimate kingship: the Wheel-treasure is won by giving to the destitute and governing by Dhamma, not inherited
Social causality sermon: an unbroken chain from neglected charity to poverty, theft, execution, civil violence and cosmic decline in lifespan
Buddhist eschatology: the sword-period of seven days as the nadir, followed by moral recovery and doubling lifespans
Maitreya prophecy: the charter of the future Buddha Metteyya, co-reigning with the wheel-king Sankha in the renewed Jambudipa
Charter of the five precepts: taught as the whole of the wheel-king's law of conquest

variants.name: Stock Wheel-Treasure narrative (DN 17 Mahasudassana; DN 19 Mahagovinda)
variants.text_tradition: Theravada, Digha Nikaya, repeated formula of the wheel-treasure appearing on the full-moon uposatha and the fourfold conquest
variants.summary: The same king-of-glory formula (wheel, elephant, horse, gem treasures; conquest by instruction rather than war) recurs in the Dialogues as portable epic formula, detached from the decline narrative.

variants.name: Anagatavamsa (Later Theravada Maitreya poem)
variants.text_tradition: Theravada, Pali kavya of uncertain date (medieval Sri Lankan), 'The Chronicle of the Future Buddha'
variants.summary: A much later, devotional expansion of the Metteyya prophecy, rich in detail on the future kingdom and cult; the canonical seed is DN 26's brief prediction.

variants.name: Three intermediate kalpas (commentarial tradition, Ledi Sayadaw)
variants.text_tradition: Theravada commentary and 20th-century abhidhamma manuals, e.g. Ledi Sadaw, Buddhist Review 1916
variants.summary: Commentaries systematize the sword-period (satthantara-kappa) as one of three calamity-intervals (famine, pestilence, sword) that fall inside a kappa, giving the sutta's scenario a scholastic frame.

secondary_sources.citation: Gethin 1998, Oxford: Oxford University Press, ch. 2 and 6 — cosmology, karma, the wheel of becoming and the Maitreya ideal.

SuttaCentral — DN 26 Pali text, commentarial notes and parallels across traditions

texts.sensitivity_guidance: Canonical scripture of a living tradition; the Metteyya (Maitreya) prophecy is an active devotional hope in Theravada communities and the sword-period passage is used in sermons about contemporary moral decline. Retell it as canonical teaching, not as a prediction about real countries or groups; do not equate the seven-day sword-period with modern war propaganda. Cite by sutta number and PTS reference.

title.en: The Mahasudassana Sutta: The Death of the Great King of Glory
title.zh: 大善見王經：大威德王之死

texts.period: Composed c. 4th-3rd c. BCE, Pali canon written 1st c. BCE; Rhys Davids translation 1910

source.work: Dialogues of the Buddha, trans. T. W. & C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1899-1921), Sutta 17 (Maha Sudassana Suttanta, Dialogues vol. II)

summary.en: Lying down to die at wattle-and-daub Kusinara, the Buddha consoles Ananda by revealing that this village was once Kusavati, royal city of the wheel-king Mahasudassana, ringed by jeweled ramparts and palm groves. The king renounces his eighty-four thousand treasuries, gives alms for seven days, dies as easily as a full man falls asleep, and is reborn in the Brahma world; the Buddha declares that he himself was that king.
summary.zh: 佛於土坯小城拘尸將滅度，慰阿難曰：此處昔為大善見王之王都俱娑婆提，七重寶牆、七行金棕櫚，王有八萬四千寶藏，臨終捨欲行施七日，如飽食者安眠而逝，生梵天；佛言彼轉輪王即我前身，此處六度埋身，諸行無常。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Kusinara death-frame is chanted at funerals and pilgrimage sites; retell respectfully; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: At Kusinara, as the Buddha lay near death, Ananda lamented that the Master should expire in this little wattle-and-daub town, a dusty jungle village. 'Say not so,' the Buddha answered: this was once Kusavati, royal city of the Great King of Glory, Mahasudassana, twelve leagues by seven, resounding day and night with ten cries, of elephants, horses and chariots, of drum, tabor and lute, of song, cymbal and gong, and the cry 'Eat, drink and be merry'; ringed by seven ramparts of gold, silver, beryl, crystal, agate, coral and all gems, with gates and pillars in the same seven metals, and seven rows of palm trees whose wind-shaken leaves made music so sweet that even drunkards and gamblers danced beneath them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 17, Maha Sudassana Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Of the king's seven treasures, the Wheel appeared on a full-moon sacred day as he kept vigil in the upper palace. Sprinkling water over it with a ceremonial pitcher, he cried 'Roll onward, O lord Wheel!' and the rival kings of east, south, west and north submitted, asking only: 'Be a Teacher to us!' His instruction was fivefold: slay no living thing; take not what is not given; act not wrongly touching bodily desires; speak no lie; drink no maddening drink. The white elephant named Changes of the Moon and the dark-maned horse Thunder-cloud bore him around the earth to its ocean boundary and back by breakfast-time; and a wondrous eight-faceted gem lit the countryside a league on every side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 17, Maha Sudassana Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: His glory culminated in the Palace of Righteousness, the Dhamma-hall that outshone his eighty-four thousand other mansions. When he lay dying, his queen Subhadda and the courtiers wept, but he told them to ask a boon instead: not to let him die smitten with longing for the treasuries. 'Give alms, make gifts, establish foundations for recluses and brahmins.' For seven days the treasurer poured out gifts; and then, enumerating his eighty-four thousand cities, palaces, elephants, chariots, gems and wives, the king admonished his kin to cast away desire, long not after life, give alms, rule righteously and keep the precepts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 17, Maha Sudassana Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then, as a man full-fed with a hearty meal grows drowsy, so were the feelings of the Great King of Glory when death came upon him, and he passed to a fresh life in the Brahma world, reigning there through ages. 'It may be, Ananda, that you think that king was another person. I at that time was the Great King of Glory.' Six times his body had been laid in this very spot; the seventh was as the righteous wheel-turning king; but nowhere in the worlds of men, gods, Mara or Brahma could a place be found for an eighth, for the Tathagata lays aside his body no more. 'How transient are all component things! Growth is their nature and decay.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 17, Maha Sudassana Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mahagovinda Sutta: The High Steward Who Taught the Way to the Gods
title.zh: 大喬文陀經：大宰相出家與教天之道路

region.en: Rajagaha, Vulture Peak frame; the story is set in the old Benares kingdom (symbolic pin at Rajagaha)
region.zh: 王舍城靈鷲山說法（故事背景為古代波羅奈國，以王舍城為象徵定位）

texts.period: Composed c. 4th-3rd c. BCE, Pali canon written 1st c. BCE; Rhys Davids translation 1910

source.work: Dialogues of the Buddha, trans. T. W. & C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1899-1921), Sutta 19 (Maha-Govinda Suttanta, Dialogues vol. II)

summary.en: Asked how long the Buddha has been great in wisdom, the god Brahma the Eternal Youth tells of the brahmin High Steward Mahagovinda, who divided the earth among seven kings, sought Brahma through four rains of meditation, met the Eternal Youth face to face, learned the way to the Brahma heaven, renounced all and led kings, brahmins and his forty wives forth, teaching the road to the world of Brahma. The Buddha declares that he himself was that High Steward.
summary.zh: 梵童子應三十三天之問，述大宰相喬文陀（喬提波羅）事：其為七王分地為七國，四安居修悲定求見梵天，面晤梵童子，得生梵天之道，遂捨相位，七王、七婆羅門、四十妻與千眾隨之出家，普以四無量心遍滿世間，教人生梵天之道。佛言彼大統領即我前生，今以八正道教人直趣涅槃。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); canonical prose is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: On Vulture Peak the gandhabba youth Five-crest visits the Buddha, and that night, before the assembly of the Thirty-Three Gods, Sakka rehearses eight truthful praises of the Exalted One. Brahma the Eternal Youth, delighted, asks in substance: for how long has the Blessed One been so great in wisdom? And to show it, he tells of the brahmin High Steward of long ago, ending his speech with an eightfold Brahma-voice that reaches every god as if addressed to him alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 19, Maha-Govinda Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the days of King Disampati, the brahmin steward Govinda, the Lord of the Herds, managed all the king's affairs; when he died, his son Jotipala, wiser than the father, was installed in his place and came to be called the High Steward. When Disampati's son Renu succeeded, the Steward, reminding the king of a promise made to six companion princes, divided the great earth into seven equal portions, planning the cities Dantapura of the Kalingas, Potana of the Assakas, Mahissati of the Avantis, Roruka of the Soviras, Mithila of the Videhas, Campa of the Angas and Benares of the Kasis. He then instructed the seven anointed kings in government and taught the sacred verses to seven wealthy brahmins and seven hundred graduates.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 19, Maha-Govinda Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: A rumor spread that the High Steward saw Brahma face to face; knowing it false, he resolved to make it true, and for four months of the rains he meditated in a new rest-house east of the city, rapt in the ecstasy of pity. The four rains passed and no Brahma came. Then Brahma the Eternal Youth, knowing his thoughts, vanished from his heaven and appeared before him, and the steward, hair on end, asked his boon: by what method can a mortal reach the immortal world of Brahma? The god answered: by eschewing all claims of me and mine, abiding in lonely calm, rapt in pity, loathing all foul things, dwelling in chastity, one reaches the heaven of Brahma.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 19, Maha-Govinda Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Steward understood 'me and mine' as renunciation, 'lonely calm' as the forest seat, and 'rapt in pity' as pervading the four quarters with a heart charged with pity; only the 'foul odours' puzzled him, and the god named anger, lies, deceit, selfishness, jealousy, greed, lust, hatred and pride as the stench that shuts men out of Brahma's heaven. Since these cannot easily be suppressed while living in the world, the Steward resigned his stewardship; and after seven days, the seven kings, the seven brahmins, the seven hundred graduates, his forty wives and many thousands besides cut hair and beard, donned yellow robes and went forth with him, and he, pervading the whole world with love, pity, sympathy and equanimity, taught his disciples the way to union with the world of Brahma. The Buddha concluded: I was that High Steward; what I taught then led only to rebirth with Brahma, but my religious life now, the Ariyan Eightfold Path, conduces wholly to detachment, cessation and Nirvana.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 19, Maha-Govinda Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Payasi Sutta: The Prince Who Denied the Other World
title.zh: 波耶西經：不信他世者的駁斥

region.zh: 憍薩羅國塞維耶城（以舍衛城為象徵定位）

texts.period: Composed c. 4th-3rd c. BCE, Pali canon written 1st c. BCE; Rhys Davids translation 1910

source.work: Dialogues of the Buddha, trans. T. W. & C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1899-1921), Sutta 23 (Payasi Suttanta, Dialogues vol. II)

summary.en: Prince Payasi of Setavya held there is no other world, no beings reborn otherwise than of parents, no fruit of good or evil deeds. The young arahant Kumara Kassapa dismantles his evidence with a chain of parables: the condemned felon, the man pulled from the mire, the blind man, the pregnant co-wife, the sealed jar, the weighed body and the conch-shell trumpet. Converted, Payasi gives grudgingly, is reborn low among the Four Great Kings, and the monk Gavampati checks his fate by spirit-sight.
summary.zh: 塞維耶王子波耶西持「無他世、無自然化生、無善惡業果」之邪見。青年羅漢童子迦葉以連環譬喻破之：死刑犯不得還鄉報信、出泥坑者不願再入、生盲不得言色無、孕婦剖腹尋嗣兩喪其命、封甕稱屍無魂可見、海螺須有吹者方鳴。波耶西信服而施，然施物粗劣，死後驗之，生四天王天下劣天宮；躬自敬施之少年烏陀羅反生三十三天。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); canonical prose is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Walking on tour in Kosala with about five hundred monks, the young arahant Kumara Kassapa halted north of Setavya in the sisapa-tree grove. There resided the chieftain Payasi, holding an evil view: 'There is neither another world, nor are there beings reborn otherwise than from parents, nor fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done.' Hearing that the famous preacher had arrived, the townsfolk streamed out to hear him, but Payasi stopped them, saying 'the Boy Kassapa' would not bewitch him; then he came himself to debate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 23, Payasi Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Payasi's evidence was that dying friends had never sent back word. Kassapa answered with parables: a condemned felon is not released to run errands before execution, so why should the keepers of the Pit release sinners; a man pulled from a mire-pit would not climb back into the stench, and the smell of man offends the gods a hundred leagues away; a human century is but one day of the Thirty-Three Gods, so friends reborn there would have no time to return; and the other world is seen by the purified divine eye, not the fleshly one, as a man born blind cannot argue colors out of existence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 23, Payasi Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kassapa then told of the brahmin's pregnant co-wife who, harried for the inheritance by her stepson, took a sword, ripped open her belly to learn the sex of the child, and destroyed both her own life and the infant's; the hasty seeker of another world, he said, does the same to himself. Payasi's soul-hunting experiments, felons sealed in jars and baked, weighed alive and strangled, dissected in every posture to catch the soul going out, were answered: living men's own souls are not seen entering or leaving at dream-time; a hot iron ball is lighter than a quenched one; and the border villagers who begged a conch-shell trumpet to 'speak' learned that sound requires a blower's breath, effort and air, as the body's acts require life, heat and consciousness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 23, Payasi Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Convinced, Payasi instituted a gift to wanderers, brahmins, the poor, wayfarers and beggars, but served gruel, broken meats and coarse ball-fringed robes that he would not have touched himself. The young brahmin Uttara, passed over at the largesse, reproached him and arranged a proper gift with his own hands. When both had died, the monk Gavampati, going for siesta to an empty acacia mansion in the heaven of the Four Great Kings, met the god Payasi, who confessed his old error, reported that Uttara had been reborn among the Thirty-Three Gods, and begged him to go tell the world of men: give your gifts thoroughly, with your own hands, and with due thought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 23, Payasi Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Janavasabha Sutta: The Ghost-King Bimbisara Reports from Heaven
title.zh: 闍那婆修經：頻婆娑羅王的天界報告

region.en: Nadika, the Brick Hall, between Vesali and Kusinara (symbolic pin at Vesali)
region.zh: 那提迦磚殿（毘舍離與拘尸城之間，以毘舍離為象徵定位）

texts.period: Composed c. 4th-3rd c. BCE, Pali canon written 1st c. BCE; Rhys Davids translation 1910

source.work: Dialogues of the Buddha, trans. T. W. & C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1899-1921), Sutta 18 (Jana-vasabha Suttanta, Dialogues vol. II)

summary.en: After many Magadhan lay disciples die, the Buddha resolves to know their fate, and a splendid spirit appears declaring itself Janavasabha, formerly King Bimbisara, now in his seventh rebirth among the retinue of the Great King Vessavana. The ghost-king reports a celestial parliament: the Thirty-Three Gods rejoicing that new arrivals from the holy life outshine them, Brahma the Eternal Youth appearing with thirty-three shapes, and a tally of Magadha's dead attaining stream-entry.
summary.zh: 摩竭陀眾多信徒新喪，佛在磚殿觀其生處。大威靈夜叉自言「我是闍那婆修」，即頻婆娑羅王，已第七次生毗沙門天王眷屬中，不復墮惡趣。其奏報天庭：三十三天集會善法堂，新從佛修聖道而生諸天光明勝舊，眾喜「天眾增長，修羅眾減」；梵童子化作三十三身宣佛德，逾二百四十萬摩竭陀亡者已入預流之數。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); canonical prose is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: At the Brick Hall of Nadika, after many Magadhan lay disciples had died, the Buddha sat resolving, by his own power, to know their after-death destiny and whither these good men were bound. An invisible spirit made himself heard crying 'I am Janavasabha! I am Janavasabha, O Welcome One!' Ananda had never heard the name and was thrilled; then the spirit appeared in splendid presence and declared: 'I am Bimbisara. 'Tis now the seventh time that I am reborn into the communion of the great King Vessavana. Deceased as a human king, I am in heaven become a non-human king; fourteen lives I know, and I am destined never to be reborn in a state of woe, and now I aspire to become a Once-returner.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 18, Jana-vasabha Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sent as Vessavana's messenger to King Virulhaka, the spirit had first come to report what the Great King had announced to his assembly. On the night of the full moon of the month Asalhi, all the gods of the Thirty-Three assembled in the Hall of Good Counsel, the Four Great Kings seated at the four quarters; and the gods newly risen in their midst because they had lived the higher life under the Exalted One outshone the others in appearance and glory, so that the assembly cried with joy: 'Verily the celestial hosts are waxing, the titanic hosts are waning!' And Sakka, and Brahma the Eternal Youth in his turn, sang the praises of the Tathagata and the cosmic law in verse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 18, Jana-vasabha Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: A splendid light then shone from the north, the herald sign of Brahma. Sanamkumara, the Eternal Youth, took on a relatively gross personality in the shape of the gandhabba youth Five-crest, rose into the air and sat cross-legged in the sky, and created thirty-three shapes of himself, seated on the couch of each of the Thirty-Three Gods, so that each god thought the voice spoke to him alone. He proclaimed the completeness of the Buddha's revelation, the Four Roads to Psychic Power and the Three Avenues to Bliss, adding the line that was to be quoted for centuries: 'Wide opened are the portals to Nirvana!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 18, Jana-vasabha Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Most marvellous of all was the tally of Magadha: more than twenty-four lacs of the Exalted One's dead disciples had, through the destruction of the three fetters, become converted, cannot be reborn in any state of woe and are assured of the Insight; of the higher breed, the non-returners, the tale could not be told without wronging the truth. This matter the spirit Janavasabha reported to the Exalted One, the Exalted One reported to Ananda, and Ananda to the brethren, the sisterhood and the lay faithful; and the System waxed influential and prosperous, and expanded and broadened with the numbers that joined, so well was it spread abroad among men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Digha Nikaya 18, Jana-vasabha Suttanta (Rhys Davids 1910); not verbatim.
